title: Question time: What makes a 'good' grind in an MMO?
summary: Hear me out, then hear me out 1,000 more times.
body: I'm about to say something controversial—I don't actually think grinds in MMOs are all that bad. There's a bit of a wider resistance to the idea of having to grind for anything in a modern online game, a resistance to the very concept, even. We've all certainly got less time than in the days of attunement questlines . But that doesn't mean an MMO can be entirely grindless, right? Depending on how you define the term, after all. They're, typically speaking, RPGs—RPGs have levels, slow-burn goals to achieve, and so on. For the sake of ease, let's just define a grind as a repetitive activity you need to do many times in a role to achieve a goal. Even then, has that sort of thing been entirely stamped out? Not exactly. We aren't quite at EverQuest levels of quests being rare breaks from the eternal mobbing, but those archetypal grinds have morphed into new forms. Battle-pass like reward tracks, seasons, world quests, or, in the case of Final Fantasy 14 , relic weapons. I recently had to sprint to catch up on my relic weapon step, which required me to gather a bunch of crystal paste from dungeons. If you're unfamiliar with FF14—basically, I had to get 600 of a thing to get a cool weapo…

title: The games industry's 'fear of risk is currently the largest risk it faces' according to Nuclear Throne's producer
summary: "Courage is a consistent factor of most hit titles."
body: With videogame budgets ballooning and competition ever intensifying there's a huge amount riding on whether a modern videogame succeeds or fails. As such, publishers are increasingly turning to the safest bets possible, like sequels in proven series or shiny remakes of classic games. It's the exact strategy that Xbox has said it's falling back on to increase its fortune—recommitting to its big names like Halo , Fallout , The Elder Scrolls etc. Admittedly, that strategy also includes laying off thousands of people and cutting ties with numerous game studios, which thus far has yielded Xbox's worst quarter in years. Indeed, rather than helping sustain the industry, this aversion to risk may be a source of its present struggles. As reported by GamesIndustry.biz , this was the conclusion of a workgroup run by Vlambeer cofounder and Nuclear Throne producer Rami Ismail at this year's DevGAMM Madeira Games Summit. Titled "We're moving fast and losing what made us good (creativity, craft & the future)", the workgroup brought together people from various corners of the games industry to discuss how to put creativity back at the heart of game dev (and game financing). title: We haven't needed motion blur in games for a long time, so I wish it would stop being the default
summary: Do you also turn it off immediately, like I do?
body: James Bentley, hardware writer (Image credit: Future) This week I've been: recovering from testing Halo: Campaign Evolved and playing far too much The Binding of Isaac. I have an experiment for you. Right now, as you stare at this article on a phone, monitor, PS Vita, whatever, spin your head around. Oh, probably don't do that in public or while walking. Or do. I don't know, I'm not your dad. But you will probably spot that the entire world doesn't go blurry as you spin. Now, a second experiment: wave your hand in front of you and tell me if your hand goes blurry. As you'll likely deduce from that very scientific experiment, motion blur (ie the entire world going blurry around you as you wiggle your head) is not a 'realistic' game setting. One of the first things I do when I play a game is turn motion blur off. Given you are reading this on PC Gamer dot com, the likelihood is that you do the same. Recently, while playing Halo: Campaign Evolved , I realised it has one of the worst implementations of motion blur I've ever seen , and it even has the audacity to be on by default. title: In happier times, Sony was courting PC gamers with lavish magazine ads for its 'most popular CD-ROM titles'
summary: Back when Sony still liked discs *and* publishing games on the PC.
body: Well well well—what a difference, uh, 30 years makes, huh? While the Sony of 2026 is insisting that it should, or must , carry on with the execution of physical media for its forthcoming PlayStation 6, and has backed away from releasing its prestige games on PC , the Sony of 1996 was in a very different mindset. Shortly after the release of the original PlayStation, Sony was still so eager to court PC gamers that it took out a 16 page ad supplement in this very magazine to hype up its "PlayStation mega-hits" with "CD-quality audio." "Sony is just as committed to bringing great games to the PC as they are to creating cutting-edge PlayStation titles," the ad reads, as it explains that storied PC publisher Psygnosis had become a subsidiary of Sony Interactive. While many of the games featured throughout the 16 page ad insert are not exactly all-timers, it's fun to look back and see a few closely associated with the PlayStation console, namely WipEout and Twisted Metal, listed for PC. title: After a year and a half of rigorous testing, Path of Exile 2 devs finally convinced Nvidia to fix a driver bug by sending it an entire PC
summary: We're finally free.
body: There was a point in the most recent Path of Exile 2 league that I thought I would have to quit playing the game. Every 20 minutes or so, the entire game would freeze. I'd wait for a solid 30 seconds before everything came back to life, praying I wouldn't lose my character the second I had control again. When I looked up why this could be happening, I found dozens of Reddit threads about the same issue. People have been suffering from intermittent freezes and crashes since the game launched in early access and the only solution was to swap a setting that made it look considerably worse until developer Grinding Gear Games figured out a solution. It turns out the freezes were just the first part of a troubleshooting saga that the developers have been on for the last year and a half. As of this week, the war against Path of Exile 2's constant GPU shader crashes is finally over thanks to a mountain of effort GGG put into diagnosing them. title: Bulletstorm is the stupidest game ever made, and also one of the cleverest shooters ever
summary: Enjoying the high-kicks and low-brows of a timeless FPS.
body: From the archives: This article originally ran in PC Gamer #330 (UK, May 2019). You should still play Bullestorm, which is frequently 90% off on Steam . Bulletstorm is the stupidest game ever made. Everything about this game is stupid. Your character is stupid. Your allies are stupid. Your enemies are very stupid. The weapons are daft. The skillshot system is absurd. The script almost prides itself on how much rank idiocy it can cram into every line. Even the setting is stupid, a holiday resort built using prison labour on an alien planet so hostile that it rains gamma radiation. You’d be forgiven for thinking that Bulletstorm was developed by semi-concussed jocks during a two-year long frat party. It makes Gears of War look sensible, an impression that is probably the main reason why it sold a pitiful number of copies when it originally released in 2011. The game has such a brash and puerile exterior that it put a lot of people off playing. That’s such a shame, because beneath the fathom-thick veneer of dumbness is one of the cleverest shooters designed this side of the millennium. Every stupid thing that Bulletstorm does has been designed with a huge amount of thought. Take the …

title: Sony exec says killing discs won't make the PlayStation 6 too much like a PC: 'Going forward, we can coexist peacefully with PC games'
summary: Despite pushback, Sony isn't changing its mind about dropping physical discs in 2028.
body: Sony's decision to end game disc production and go fully digital in 2028 was met with no small amount of backlash. Concerns range from loss of the ability to trade in old games on new ones to the potential inability to play games when services are offline—which happens—or accounts are lost, not to mention the basic principle of the thing: What do you really own if your ownership is dependent upon the whims of a distant digital platform? Despite that pushback, Sony isn't changing its mind: During the company's latest earnings call , chief financial officer Lin Tao said she knows people have "strong views" on the topic, but so does Sony, and its view is that it's going to happen. "There are various reasons we made this decision," Tao said in response to an analyst's question about the driving factors behind the change. "The biggest being that the digitalization of contents overall has been progressing. That's the big factor. "It's not just for PlayStation, but for all kinds of contents, digitalization is progressing, and so when we think about the future, we put in a lot of thought and time. We cautiously considered this, we came to this conclusion, and we're going to cautiously mov…

body: One of the most magical parts of Silent Hill f was that never in a hundred years did I think it would be something that Konami would greenlight . Not because it's outlandish or a poor idea, I absolutely loved it, but because I just thought Konami had kind of set aside doing anything new with the franchise. But I was wrong, and I've never been happier to be wrong, because Silent Hill f was exactly the kind of shake up this series needed—adding new twists to what we've come to expect from these games while also holding its psychological horror roots from Silent Hill 2 sacred. title: It seems like AMD's Zen 6 LP CPU cores will be a mixture of architectures going all the way back to Zen 2
summary: I'd love to see these thrown into a gaming laptop.
body: As we reported last month, AMD is working on a low-power, compact range of Zen 6 CPUs , which should be perfect for inclusion in laptops and gaming handhelds. If you're wondering how it plans on doing that, it seems the answer is a collage of different Zen architectures from Zen 2 upwards combined. As spotted by industry analyst InstLatX64 (via Wccftech ), a Linux kernel patch from Vishal Badole, a member of AMD staff, notes that the low-power core is marked in CPUID. This designation, distinct from a regular Zen 'C' core, is necessary for the following reasons, according to the patch: "user space exposure via /sys/kernel/debug/x86/topo/cpus/*, which today reports cpu_type "unknown" for low-power cores amd_get_boost_ratio_numerator(): on every X86_FEATURE_AMD_HTR_CORES-capable AMD/Hygon part, low-power cores must scale by amd_get_highest_perf() rather than the fixed CPPC_HIGHEST_PERF_PERFORMANCE ceiling, matching the existing efficiency-core path" According to InstLatX64, the low-power core is a "collage CPU", made up of a Zen 6 ISA, Zen 5 uArch [microarchitecture], Zen 4 FPU, Zen 3 L2 and a Zen 2 L3 cache. title: I made a hyper organised plant shop in Leafy Corner because the people want order not whimsy
summary: I wonder if this'll translate into keeping my own plants alive.
body: I am lucky enough to live close to some of the best plant shops I've ever had the pleasure to stumble into. I love taking my sweet time strolling around each one, looking at all the plants, succulents, seeds, and pots—all of which I could never dream of fitting into my small apartment. The best part of all of them is just how jumbled they all are, brimming with all sorts of strange plants for customers to discover. So, with that in mind you'd think I'd also create a maze-oasis of foliage right? Wrong. The plant shop I created in Leafy Corner, the management sim game which just released, is regimented and ordered. Pots are colour coded and plants are separated into strict categories. You see, the whimsy will be better accessible if everything is ordered clearly. summary: We'll have to test one for ourselves to make up our minds.
body: I'm likely not the first to tell you that the memory crisis has really done a number on PC gaming, but nothing quite exemplifies this like AMD releasing a graphics card with 4-8 GB of VRAM in 2026. That card is called the RX 9050 ; it starts at $279, and it is limited to certain regions. One early review suggests performance isn't great, but its specs are looking a little funky. That review is from Japanese hardware outlet Hermitage Akihabara , which managed to get its hands on an 8 GB-toting ASRock model. Testing the card in 3DMark, Hermitage argues it "falls short of the 30fps generally considered the benchmark for comfortable single-player gameplay. Furthermore, its performance is only about 75% of that of its competitor, the GeForce RTX 5050, and just over 60% compared to the higher-end Radeon RX 9060 XT" (machine translated). The RX 9050 doesn't lag behind the RTX 5050 in absolutely all tests, though. The RX 9050 matches the RTX 5050 in 4K testing on Rainbow Six Siege X, and it performed better in Doom Eternal at 1080p and 1440p, though this was with the help of FSR, which is not an apples-to-apples comparison. Still, the RTX 5050 wipes the floor with the RX 9050 in pretty mu…

title: Report shows 34% of physical PS5 games and 50% of Xbox Series X games do not work fully without a download first
summary: Are consoles following PC's lead?
body: Sony is getting ready to end production of game discs in 2028 , so it seems like physical discs are truly in the rearview mirror. But a recent report shows even buying a physical disc doesn't give you a great chance of being able to play the game without a download. That's according to Does it Play (via Ars Technica ), which is an outlet dedicated to testing the physical versions of games to see if you can play them offline or without a download. It has a statistics function on its home page that allows you to scroll through different consoles and check out how offline-friendly they are. As you might expect, Sony and Microsoft's latest consoles don't fare too well. For PS5, Does it Play registers 792 games and states that 66% of them don't need any sort of download to play the game as intended. 17% are categorised as being beatable but being too buggy or missing central content, while a further 17% need some sort of download to actually play the game. Microsoft fares even worse, with the Series X only getting the pass for 50% of tested games. 12% are in the too buggy to play or missing content but technically beatable camp, with 68% needing some sort of download to play. body: Capcom is on a roll. It had a successful year, what with the release of Resident Evil Requiem and Pragmata, the latter of which sold 2.5 million copies in just three months. "One of the reasons for creating remakes is producing a new entry in the Resident Evil series every year would be quite an undertaking and a difficult task," producer Masachika Kawata says in an interview with GameInformer . "So, being able to revisit older games and remake them helps Capcom meet that goal of releasing a Resident Evil title each year, but it also allows the team to continually challenge themselves and hone their craft. title: Mchose K7 V2 Ultra+ review
summary: Great specs with a Viper V3/V4 Pro's shape, for less.
body: I've been a very happy chappy ever since discovering the wonders of the Chinese 'clone' mouse market. Brands in this market attempt to deliver quality gaming mice that take after popular shapes by mainstream brands, but for a lot less money. I was sceptical at first, but my experience with Mchose mice has squashed my scepticism, and this K7 V2 Ultra+ is a fine example. It is, for all intents and purposes, a Razer Viper V3/V4 Pro clone, and the latter is currently the absolute best gaming mouse on the market today. I say V3/V4 Pro because it sits between the two, using an overclocked PixArt PAW3955 TI sensor that hits up to 50,000 DPI. That's PixArt's flagship market-available sensor, and the Razer Viper V4 Pro has its own top-of-the-line, custom PixArt sensor that has the same DPI as this but higher IPS capability and so on. Still, the K7 V2's sensor is flagship as far as what is actually on the market. Regarding just the shape, I notice no difference between this and the Viper V4 Pro, which tracks, given EloShapes shows no difference either. There is, of course, a difference in build quality (and no optical switches), but that's less to do with the Mchose and more to do with the …

body: Baldur's Gate 3 proved that the rules of Dungeons & Dragons, with some tweaks, make a brilliant framework for a videogame RPG. And yet Wizards of the Coast seems intent on making games that don't use that framework. Last year the publisher announced Invoke, one of its internal videogame studios, was making Warlock, a third-person action adventure that seems like an attempt at making their own God of War. Warlock may well turn out to be a decent game, it's just odd that while I'm sure Wizards of the Coast will find a studio it trusts to make Baldur's Gate 4 eventually, it's not interested in making another game like it only without the words "Baldur's Gate" in the name in the meantime. We still don't know much about Warlock, but WotC did use its D&D keynote at Gen Con to reveal that Maggie Robertson, who portrayed Lady Dimitrescu in Resident Evil Village and Orin the Red in Baldur's Gate 3, will be playing the protagonist's patron. Like every warlock, you'll get your powers from a pact with a supernatural benefactor, in this case the witch Tasha of Tasha's Hideous Laughter fame. title: Dark Sun, D&D's most heavy metal setting, will be back in 2027
summary: Finally, a survival game where I don't have to punch trees.
body: Look, it was the 1990s. Everybody was super into two things: edginess, and caring deeply about the environment. A Dungeons & Dragons setting where the entire world had been turned into a hostile desert wasteland by exploitative sorcerer-kings and a bunch of sinewy warriors with psychic powers and an aversion to pants had to slaughter each other to survive was perfect for the zeitgeist. Though Dark Sun was briefly brought back as part of D&D's 4th edition, a revival for the current 5th edition has been in demand for a while now. Public playtests of the psion, a class first created for Dark Sun, have kept the rumor mill churning, and at Gen Con's D&D keynote Wizards of the Coast finally pressed the big red button that said "dark fantasy nostalgia for '90s kids" and announced its return. Dark Sun will be getting a rulebook aimed at players called Blood and Power with the psion class in it, as well as a setting guide aimed at Dungeon Masters called Edge of Oblivion. A special printing of the Player's Handbook with Dark Sun's distinctive gore-soaked Wrestlemania art is also planned. All three are scheduled for release next year. title: The mod we called 'the best Fallout game you'll play this year' back in 2018 just launched on GOG
summary: If you missed it back then, it's easier than ever to play it now.
body: Fallout 4 remaster, Fallout: New Vegas remaster, Fallout 5, Fallout 3 prequel for Fallout 76, Fallout (the TV series) Season 3, and whatever Fallout game Obsidian is now working on … there's a whoooooole lotta Fallout coming your way if you're a Fallout fan. But, uh, not for a while. What's a Jet junkie to do in the meantime? Well, how about Fallout: New California, a full conversion mod for Fallout: New Vegas that just released on GOG . Here's the trailer. Fallout: New California may have just appeared on GOG but it's not so much new as it is newly accessible . The project has been around for quite a while, and if you don't believe me, we called it " the best Fallout game you'll play this year " way back in 2018—and at that stage it had already been in development for roughly seven years, originally called Project Brazil. Officially hosted now on GOG, it can now be installed and launched easily if you own Fallout: New Vegas Ultimate Edition, rather than downloading the files and other half-dozen recommended mods through Moddb and managing the install yourself. title: The rumors were true, Dungeons & Dragons' first 'Universes Beyond' crossover will be with World of Warcraft
summary: Finally, I can catch the Corrupted Blood plague in person.
body: Dungeons & Dragons has been publishing rules for other settings going way back, with Conan adventures in 1984 and Lankhmar – City of Adventure in 1985. Even further back in 1980, the first printing of Deities & Demigods included stats for gods from Michael Moorcock's Elric stories and H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu mythos. It's even collaborated with Blizzard on a line of Diablo supplements to tie in with the release of Diablo 2. So it's not too shocking that the first official Dungeons & Dragons crossover book released as part of its Universes Beyond line (borrowing the name from Magic: The Gathering, where crossovers have been big earners) will be about World of Warcraft. Especially since the news already leaked over the weekend . The announcement was formalized at this year's Gen Con, where Wizards of the Coast put on a D&D Vision Keynote 2027 presented by Theo Solomon (who played Wyll in Baldur's Gate 3). We'll be getting a 256-page hardcover book with rules for 11 new species, 9 subclasses (6 of them new, 3 updated versions of existing characters), 50+ new monsters, 60+ new spells, 23 factions, 7 dungeons, 26 magic items including artifacts, and stat blocks for various popular cha…

title: Saudi Arabia's $55 billion takeover of Electronic Arts will happen next week
summary: EA says all regulatory hurdles are cleared, so all that's left to do is to do it.
body: Bad news for anyone holding out hope that some power-on-high would swoop in and put a halt to Saudi Arabia's takeover of Electronic Arts : A new Form 8-K filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission says the deal has green lights across the board, and will be done next week. More formally, "as of July 30, 2026, all regulatory approvals required to complete the Merger have been obtained," the filing states. "Electronic Arts currently expects the Merger to close on or about the close of trading on August 4, 2026. Completion of the Merger remains subject to the satisfaction or waiver of the remaining customary closing conditions set forth in the Merger Agreement." Realistically, I don't think anyone expected that this proposed takeover by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund would run into too many obstacles. The Federal Trade Commission fought like hell when Microsoft acquired Activision Blizzard, and ultimately lost; the PIF takeover of EA seems far less likely to trigger concerns about competition, because it's not a merger of two game makers into one bigger game maker, but rather a change in ownership. title: There's a timeline where Dark Souls was a PlayStation exclusive, but Sony lost out on the chance because it wouldn't publish Demon's Souls in North America
summary: Things could always be worse.
body: First reported by 4Gamer (with translation by Automaton ), former Sony Interactive Entertainment executive Shuhei Yoshida recently spoke about Sony's decision not to publish Demon's Souls in North America, which led FromSoftware to partner with Bandai Namco on its breakout 2011 hit, Dark Souls. Yoshida provided the keynote address at this year's CEDEC industry conference in Japan, where he spoke about some of his experiences working close to the top of Sony's games business. Sony published Demon's Souls in Japan⁠—hence its console-exclusive status to this day⁠—but declined to bring the game oversees. According to Yoshida, Demon's Souls' initial Japanese run only consisted of 20,000 copies shipped, and it was not expected to break even on development costs. Trying the game for himself in 2008, a year before launch, Yoshida said he failed to make much progress after two hours, and described his conclusion as "what an unfriendly game." To be fair to Yoshida, this is more or less identical to my first experience with Demon's Souls as well. But Demon's Souls went on to have strong sales and word of mouth in Japan, leading Atlus and Bandai Namco to handle its distribution in other regio…

body: In a time when the dominant game engines are contorting themselves to accommodate generative AI toolsets and the resurrected specter of NFTs, game developers who might be investigating alternatives should be asking themselves one very important, yet all too often overlooked question: Does this engine's built-in scripting language allow me to write code using the finest and most adaptive logo-syllabic writing system ever devised in ancient Mesopotamia? title: Has 'Xbox 360 brown' nostalgia finally arrived?
summary: Mid-2000s grittiness may be due a comeback.
body: Will anyone ever reminisce fondly about the 2026 Toyota Camry? It seems impossible. Today's cars are almost all ugly to me, and the exceptions are usually concept cars that mimic the lines of decades past. And yet, on an intellectual level, I know that perspectives on this will change. My first car was a 1990 Toyota Camry that was not at all cool when I was driving it around in the 2000s. Now? It may not be a coveted collector's item, but someone recently got over 900 upvotes on Reddit for showing off a well-maintained specimen. A few days ago I asked you guys about a 1990 Camry, and today picked her up. It's in immaculate condition, especially since it's 34 years old from r/Toyota A little later in the 2000s, when I was driving a different uncool car, everyone was making fun of "Xbox 360 brown," a trend toward muddy, desaturated colors (brown, green, grey, "piss") and ultra-gritty games (they said swears, even). title: Blizzard is keeping secrets about Diablo 4's next season until BlizzCon, but you can still try some of it out next week
summary: There are still plenty of new toys to play with though.
body: For the first time in three years, we're not getting advance notice on absolutely everything coming in the next Diablo 4 season. Usually, Blizzard spells it all out in the patch notes, but this time it's keeping its lips sealed until BlizzCon in September. There's still a good amount of stuff to see in the season 15 blog post , including new seasonal items, returning items from past games, and further changes to the controversial Mythic Unique item changes from last season. But there are two sections that look suspiciously empty, suggesting that the full reveals will happen on stage at BlizzCon. The first of these are called "Challenge Dungeons", which seem to be boss encounters that randomly appear while you're exploring the open world. Blizzard specifically says you'll enter these new portals to "fight against a fearsome boss" and that the difficulty level will be customizable once you're well into the endgame. My first thought after reading about the Challenge Dungeons is that they might be a permanent version of the current season's Deathtoll Chambers. title: This upcoming Steam game is pioneering the accursed trucking genre, and as a former delivery guy I could not be more thrilled
summary: Prospice: Anomalous Logistics simulates the canonical deliveryman experience of having your dreambody dissolved in the labyrinth of collective death.
body: As a former delivery guy, I have a fondness in my heart for videogame trucking. It lets me reclaim the simple satisfaction of moving things where they need to go without needing to endure all the things that make people glad they aren't a delivery guy. There's just one problem: Videogame truckin' isn't weird enough. My six years of delivery work regularly involved surreal events, uncanny individuals, inexplicable decisions, and plenty of other inscrutable encounters. Videogame trucking, however, tends to be extremely scrutable—until this week, when developer Code Wakers launched an open playtest for Prospice: Anomalous Logistics , an upcoming driving and delivery sim that's properly unfathomable. (Image credit: Forklift Interactive) In Prospice, you play as an employee of an organization that would be right at home alongside the SCP Foundation, the Federal Bureau of Control, and any number of groups poking around the Backrooms. Its mission is researching an island that is, in the Steam description's words, "cursed by the corpses of ever rotting gods" and "a place where the world itself unravels." Unfortunately, the open wilderness isn't the best environment for researching the rem…

title: Dbrand unveils Steam Machine customization 'backup plan' after its Companion Cube got confined to the test chamber
summary: That's a wrap.
body: The Steam Machine is finally here—though Dbrand's Companion Cube-inspired skin for it will sadly never see light outside of a test chamber. Turns out, the peripherals and accessories brand had ' built the idea into something real without ever asking Valve' for permission . But Dbrand has now rocked up with what it's describing as its 'backup plan.' This week, Dbrand unveiled a suite of Steam Machine skins . The most expensive are the genuinely fuzzy ' Touch Grass ' skin and the ' Real Black Leather ' wrap, which each cost $60. Besides that, Dbrand's Steam Machine skins range in price from about $43 for the more complexly patterned wraps, to about $35 for the single colour skins. I'm personally quite partial to this one with an all-over marbling effect —of course, it also helps Dbrand call it 'Cotton Candy'. What I'm much less a fan of is some of the acerbic advertising copy on the skins' page. Dbrand describes its Steam Machine wraps as "Thin—Unlike you." C'mon, now. The skins' width is then described as about two hair's breadth thick, though this little factoid comes wrapped in digs about hair loss that are simply not funny. title: Thimbleweed Park 2 is 'not really a sequel, not really a prequel,' but it is finally happening
summary: Ron Gilbert says the next game in the now-a-series is set to come out in early 2028.
body: Released in 2017, Thimbleweed Park is a LucasArts-style point-and-click adventure about murder in a small town, headed up by LucasArts veterans Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick. All that LucasArts pedigree added up to an 84% score in our review , on the strength of "challenging puzzles, oddball characters, and an intriguing, mystery-laden plot"—and of course the familiar visual style that immediately conjures thoughts of Monkey Island, Day of the Tentacle, and Zak McCracken. It's taken a decade (almost a decade, anyway, and it will be more than that when it happens) but a sequel is finally happening. Gilbert revealed on his Grumpy Gamer blog that Thimbleweed Park 2 is now in early development, and it's set to launch in early 2028. People from the original Thimbleweed Park dev team including Mark Ferrari, Gary Winnick, David Fox, Octavi Navarro, and Robert Megone are returning to the new project, and it will be available for Windows, Mac, and Linux, on both Steam and GOG. Agents Ray and Reyes, the leads of the original game, are also back for the new game—and so is murder. title: Where to find Hirosaki Castle in Forza Horizon 6
summary: Snap a photo for the Classy Castle challenge.
body: While finding the Hokubu Treasure Hunt is undoubtedly the harder of the exploration challenges this week in Forza Horizon 6 , locating Hirosaki Castle isn't easy either. It doesn't help that the cold front has come in and covered the whole map in a blanket of snow. So, here's what you need to do. Forza Horizon 6 Hirosaki Castle location Xbox Xbox You can find Hirosaki Castle in the northeast of the Takashiro region , not far from the eastern edge of the map. Look for the Hirosaki Castle speed trap event at the centre of the area, as this will place you right out at the castle's gates, though the Hirosaki Scramble dirt race is nearby too. Plus, since it's a tourist site, it's a marked, named location on your map. To complete the Classy Castle photo challenge specifically, you need to take a photo of any classic sports car outside the castle. This includes cars like the Mazda RX-3, Chevrolet Corvette, and Nissan Skyline 2000GT-R Barn Find . Chances are you've already got something that fits the bill, so go to your garage and filter it by classic sports cars and take your pick. For your hard work as a car photographer, you'll earn two Festival Playlist points and the White Suit cloth…
